title: Revolt of the Credentialed Masses
author: https://hedgehogreview.com/contributors/justin-vassallo
text:
For a brief period following the COVID-19 shock, the American left became convinced that the labor movement was on the cusp of a generational revival. As documented across a series of vignettes in Mutiny: The Rise and Revolt of the College-Educated Working Class, a new book by Noam Scheiber, a labor reporter at the New York Times, younger hourly shift workers in retail, food service, shipping, and technology were at the forefront of this new surge in workplace organizing. At first, most did not fancy themselves activists. Nor did they anticipate taking on powerful and famous global American brands such as Starbucks, Apple, and Amazon—firms that had easily dispatched previous organizing drives. But as their jobs became more tedious and the pandemic introduced new hazards and complications that betrayed the growing vacuity of their employers’ “values,” these workers became hardened organizers determined to win concessions and spread collective bargaining to neglected frontiers.

This rebellion was sparked not merely by meager pay or onerous new procedures but also by career disappointment and disillusionment of a kind not normally associated with blue-collar workers. These twenty-something workers were different in one important way from what’s left of unionized industrial labor and many of their already unionized counterparts in the hospitality sector: They were, as Scheiber writes, college graduates whose professional opportunities fell far short of what universities and American culture had primed them to expect. They were thus emblematic of precarious or downwardly mobile Millennials (and their Gen-Z successors): burdened by college debt, struggling to afford rent and other routine bills, and increasingly resigned to doing jobs that were, at best, tenuously connected to the roles they had aspired to secure. 

By their own admission, the process of radicalization unfolded in stages. Although they were liberal-minded, these workers at the margins of the knowledge economy were neither militant nor even especially political when they entered the labor market in the 2010s. In fact, some initially admired the companies for which they worked because of those companies’ public commitments to “corporate responsibility” and “progressive” benefits, such as the company stock and health insurance Starbucks offered. Chaya Barrett, a black organizer at the Apple Store in Towson, Maryland, was an Apple enthusiast who once hoped to ascend the corporate ladder. Only a few prominent organizers, such as Jaz Brisack of Starbucks Workers United, in Buffalo, New York, were so-called “salts” who sought to get hired for the purpose of organizing a union. 

As educated, responsible workers who exuded a sense of drive and ambition, they might have been expected to conceal their percolating discontent. But it was precisely because of their education, Scheiber argues, that workers who felt used and undervalued were apt to scrutinize how power was wielded by their employers. They then connected their struggles to the frustrations and demands that had fueled Occupy Wall Street and Bernie Sanders’s campaigns for president. After years of swallowing various on-the-clock indignities while profits and CEO compensation continued to soar, this disenchanted cohort came to understand themselves as part of the working class.

For Scheiber and others who hailed them as the new face of the labor movement, this awakening to the fundamental division in American society was an auspicious sign. A seemingly interminable and caustic debate over class and identity had roiled the left during the 2010s, but the sense of momentum generated by the organizing drives demonstrated that young progressives grasped the unique importance of labor politics when challenging the powerful. Among idealists, this development suggested political and sociocultural polarization along regional and educational lines might be finite and that a New Deal–style coalition could still be forged in the twenty-first century. It showed, moreover, that the repertoire of the trade-union-aligned “Old Left” could be reclaimed by a “new” New Left, thereby answering critics who saw it as a histrionic and self-righteous creature of elite colleges. 

As Scheiber writes, these possibilities exist because the process of “proletarianization” among the college-educated is, at bottom, quite real. Against the prevailing wisdom, in which polarization is said to reflect and calcify important “class-based” differences between degree-holders and the “non-college-educated,” Scheiber suggests there is not much separating the lower strata of the “Brahmin left”—the educated, mostly urban and coastal base of the modern Democratic Party—from those Trump-leaning, less-educated workers who have seen their life chances evaporate across the Rust Belt. Both confront a daily reality in which middle-class stability has become elusive and economic predation is omnipresent. In an economy bifurcated between the high-income, asset-rich class and “paycheck-to-paycheck” households, the distinctions between occupations and education levels are therefore much less relevant to class status than they had been in the previous industrial epoch. What matters for party politics is that the new, degree-holding precariat genuinely understands its hardships as representative of a larger, captured system that has, since the Reagan Revolution, ruthlessly redistributed wealth and power upward.

Mutiny, however, has a narrower tale to tell than is suggested by the title, which conjures the image of a groundswell revolt across industries. The showdowns with management and strikes Scheiber recounts are hardly akin to the tumult and proletarian radicalism of the Gilded Age or the late 1930s. Scheiber vividly traces the evolution of class-consciousness among Starbucks, Apple, and Amazon organizers, as well as the simmering resentment of devalued TV and movie writers, actors, and crew members, who were alert early on to the deskilling and displacement AI has begun to inflict in sectors populated by degree-holders. Yet this movement, if it can be properly labeled as such, remains underdeveloped, susceptible to the burnout, atomization, and rootlessness that are characteristic of the industries Scheiber’s Young Turks strove to dignify.

Indeed, Mutiny is a sobering chronicle of intermittent to barely perceptible progress in sectors whose structure—that is, their operating systems and business models—typically thwarts decisive shop-floor disruption and precludes the growth of worker solidarity. Part-time positions are ubiquitous, scheduling software meant to curb labor costs often keeps staff camaraderie to a minimum, and the supply chains for the actual product that accompanies the personalized service “experience,” whether it’s a Starbucks latte or an iPhone, are largely located overseas, robbing workers here of control over the far more significant pressure points in our “postindustrial” economy. It should not be lost on readers that during the 2023 “strike wave”—the most significant period of work stoppages since 1983, though nowhere near the scale of those in the 1970s—the biggest threat to the status quo emerged from the revitalized and newly militant United Auto Workers, which, despite the dramatic decline in manufacturing employment, could still catalyze a domino effect throughout the economy on a scale no army of Starbucks baristas ever could. These conditions make it difficult to build a union and are just as likely to cause apathy and withdrawal as they are to spark confrontation with the bosses. 

Service-sector companies that pay low wages generally don’t retain workers for long, which is partly by design but also reflects a broader cultural shift in attitudes toward work that belies corporate America’s fuzzy, inclusive language about “partners,” “creatives,” and “associates.” Unlike manufacturers and other large firms at the height of welfare capitalism, there is little mutual expectation that young staff will attain seniority. Expendability is a feature, not a bug, of the business strategies of today’s chain stores and customer-facing monopolies.

And so, as prospects for upward mobility dwindle—both within individual companies and across the economy—younger workers have become more itinerant and unlikely to stay at the same shop or company for more than a couple years. They move around, take informal side gigs, moonlight in other fields undergoing a similar process of “flexibilization” and algorithm-determined extraction, and even dabble in “sugar dating” and sex work. Their résumés fill up with variations on the same basic tasks, sometimes enhanced by a title like “shift supervisor” or “assistant manager” that telegraphs reliability to prospective employers. Few, though, have the resolve to overcome sector-specific obstacles and form a union. Those who do are aware that disgruntlement with management, pay, and abusive customers does not necessarily translate into pro-union sentiment. Most of their fellow workers have little appetite to take the risk when it would be easier to jump ship for a different (though similarly unglamorous) job. 

Some of these stubborn and demoralizing aspects of the service sector are reflected in Scheiber’s intimate reporting. Mutiny is peppered with anecdotes that provide a snapshot of how corporate strategy evolved at behemoths like Apple, Starbucks, and Amazon, and how the most lavish visions of the consumer experience—the qualities and enticements which engender brand loyalty and motivate unseasoned workers in their early days on the job—are inevitably degraded in the quest to wring out larger profits.

Still, the larger context, including the dynamics that make progress toward collective bargaining so elusive in key industries, is mostly absent. Scheiber ably distills the essence of these workplace struggles, but the lack of an overarching account for why working-class and debt-ridden graduates are perpetually squeezed makes Scheiber’s otherwise worthy treatment somewhat underwhelming. This is not a mere academic quibble, considering Scheiber’s big-picture thesis: It is a question of whether the phenomenon Scheiber explores signifies what he thinks it does, and whether he has an answer for why, after nearly two decades of brazen corporate malfeasance, populist unrest, and political insurgencies, American social democracy feels as far off as ever. Scheiber only gestures to the political economy that has enabled subtler and more technologically sophisticated forms of exploitation, leaving the reader to speculate, rather pessimistically, about how much the new wave of labor organizing might accomplish without political allies who are determined to enshrine countervailing power through the law and law enforcement.

That doesn’t detract from the strength of Mutiny’s testimony to the clear possibilities of sustained collective action in a world of fleeting commitments and theatrical, online activism (what the political theorist Anton Jäger calls “hyperpolitics”). But it does deepen the impression Scheiber has overly idealized the agency of his protagonists. He seems genuinely convinced that the “revolt,” though it has ebbed nationally amid an extended hiring freeze, augurs new opportunities for progressive populism. He highlights recent opinion polls that show that public support for unions has reached its highest level since the 1960s, as well as how social media is raising the profile of organizing drives. “When Americans looked out across the workplace,” he writes, “they did not see one job as more virtuous than another. They did not distinguish between the staid dignity of autoworkers and the preening entitlement of Hollywood actors. Increasingly, the distinction they cared most about was the one between management and labor, and they overwhelmingly backed labor.” The potential for a commonality of interests is no doubt great. At some point, one desperately hopes, the public will cease tolerating the scale of the flagrant, boastful avarice of Trump’s world and its business allies.

Yet Scheiber’s assertion elides one important difference between college graduates disabused of their professional dreams and those who never had any to begin with. Much of the younger precariat feels overqualified for the jobs they do, and their newfound militancy stems, in part, from dashed expectations. Although this does not make their situation any less sympathetic, it contrasts with the average non-college-educated worker, who, before globalization, accepted doing grueling or monotonous jobs on the expectation that the pay—at least at a unionized or paternalistic company—would furnish middle-class goods and security. Steady work, under the old Fordist order, fostered pride and (a begrudging) loyalty because of what it could provide: the “American dream.” And it was the ability to provide for a family and be a community member in good standing that conferred status to ordinary people who were not acculturated to measure their self-worth in terms of professional advancement. Put another way, having money and purchasing power were (and remain) more important to the “traditional” working class than prestige—which was, by definition, rare and rarefied. This wasn’t because industrial workers were crassly materialistic but because a good wage and benefits package meant the difference between dignified comfort and the habits of mere survival that had defined their forebears. To resort to strike action, accordingly, was to fight to protect what the labor movement had achieved—but it also meant putting a lot more on the line than today’s young and unattached workers are accustomed to doing.

Today, “working-class prosperity” has become, once more, an oxymoron; vast segments of the working class are underemployed and have been stripped of their means of belonging, at both the local and national level. In our fissured knowledge-and-services economy, status is derived much more strongly from where you went to school and where you end up afterward. Of course, the college-educated precariat might reject this standard and express solidarity with those who have even less than they do. Material conditions are just as important to degree-holders buffeted by predatory rental practices, junk fees, and the debilitating cost of groceries, and they increasingly experience the same existential dread of being perpetually broke that afflicts the less-educated and dispossessed. Yet the premium placed on education, even for fairly entry-level work, has imposed a dividing line between the credentialed and those with no social capital to speak of, who are usually condemned, like new poor immigrants, to the worst and least-remunerative jobs available. For now, that has less-than-encouraging implications for the kind of political coalition that is necessary to arrest the country’s descent into oligarchy. 

Scheiber nevertheless ventures a more optimistic conclusion, underscoring that throughout history, “political unrest, even revolution, has ensued once the college-educated make common cause with the working class and the poor.” The Iran War–induced price shock that is expected to envelop the world economy, combined with the much-feared effects of AI, may well accelerate the rebellion tantalizingly glimpsed in Scheiber’s capsule. The question is how long a political establishment that has only superficially modified its essentially neoliberal character can delay it—and whether the revolt will remain episodic or at last gather enough force to attain a new settlement. As clear as the stakes are, history suggests it will take a cataclysm greater than a pandemic to transform the social contract.
